rationale: The cannabinoid arm had at least one fall in 4 of 31 participants versus 3 of 30 on placebo. Both formulations contained strawberry extract and neither assigned raw fruit. The count is people with a fall, with no recurrent-event rate or strawberry estimate.
The strawberry-containing group pools seven fruits and has adjusted HR 1.00 (95% CI 0.98 to 1.03) per 20 g/day for fall-related admissions. No separate fruit, Parkinson stratum or total fall count.

Six fruits were assigned together. The primary relevant reported postural sway comparison was inconclusive (time by phase p=.457). The 2021 registration and the article describe the same crossover. No strawberry-only or falls contrast.

Gait speed improved with the nutrient formula compared to maltodextrin. Strawberry and vanilla flavors were available in both arms. The 140-person registration and 127-person outcome analysis describe one trial, with no fall-frequency result by flavor.

Freeze-dried whole strawberry and placebo showed no group effect on fear of falling (p=.518). The entry screen excluded recent fallers. Gait, balance and fear differ from observed fall frequency. The erratum reports the same cohort.

The registered 47-person trial chose gait speed and excluded recent unexplained falls. The likely companion USDA project records do not add an independent result. Registry and project reports provide no outcome.

The current registry and original protocol describe the same isolated-fisetin trial after breast cancer chemotherapy. A fall question is planned alongside gait distance. No outcome results have posted.
The prevention cohort showed a tissue dopamine response but no reported strawberry improvement in the Figure 5 water-maze contrasts. Extract diet, experimental aging and no spontaneous fall measure.

This distinct reversal cohort assigned strawberry extract in older rats. Only blueberry showed improvement on reported rod-walk and rotarod comparisons. Strawberry neurochemical findings cannot supply a fall sign.
Author abstract reports no reversal of aged-mouse motor-test deficits. Arm-level results remain open. This species and design are distinct from the two rat studies. No raw fruit or clinical falls.

High-dose leaf extract prolonged mouse rotarod latency and shortened pole turning. The reported cell-line experiment overlaps the poster. Leaves and test performance provide no transferable raw fruit and spontaneous fall direction.
A strawberry odor item showed nominal group discrimination and did not enter the final three-item panel. The grouping is freezing status. The study does not compare eaten fruit or falls.

Adequate combined produce corresponds to lower adjusted odds of previously reported injurious falls. The female and male estimates differ materially. The pooled exposure, recall and absence of a Parkinson stratum leave no strawberry effect.
Daily fruit and vegetable consumption is associated with lower adjusted odds of prior-year falls (OR 0.55). No strawberry identity, separate fruit estimate or Parkinson population.
Case-control dietary comparisons use aggregate fruit frequency, with cases defined by fractures after falls. There is no species-specific or recurring Parkinson fall contrast.
Seasonal strawberry consumption is observed in the underlying diet and microbiota cohort. Diet is measured rather than assigned and no fruit-only or fall outcome is reported.

rationale: Wild strawberries appear as traditional First Foods. The source documents food use and access without reporting a symptom outcome or first-person efficacy observation.

The later poster reports 38.53 versus 23.58 autoshaping trials per 60 minutes with milkshake versus peanut oil. The 13-animal milkshake group likely overlaps the ASN poster and exact cohort lineage remains unverified. This result concerns engagement, with distinct food formulations and no fall endpoint.
All applicable task groups receive the same milkshake reward. The original paper measures cue approaches and related neural signaling and provides no comparative strawberry or fall outcome.

The food-related dermatology entries discuss strawberry alongside other possible reaction triggers. The definitions provide no inspectable fruit-specific outcome comparison or fall frequency. Descriptive clinical terms are separate.

P-557 and the fuller published article share the three fruit extracts and investigators. Relative membrane findings depend on the measured property and model. These are applied extracts in laboratory tests with no mobility result.

The linked P-603 and authors' paper use strawberry leaf extracts in red-cell or model-membrane assays. Exact sample overlap is uncertain. A cell or model result supplies no oral fruit fall comparison.

Two or more weekly strawberry servings versus less than one favored the adjusted cognitive slope by 0.03 standard units (95% CI 0.00 to 0.06). Preparation, fall counts and Parkinson-specific estimates are unavailable.
The laboratory preparation comparison studies four other wild berries. The strawberry details trace to separate animal and human references rather than these assays.

The older-adult survey reports strawberry-flavored supplement preference. The falls findings printed on the same page are from a separate vitamin D analysis. There is no assignment or falls estimate for the strawberry exposure.

The grouped strawberry, cherry and grape report compares overeating-related responses by food-addiction status. Preparation and individual fruit are unresolved. No fall outcome or Parkinson population is reported.

The recovered original compares three oil-based diet periods using processed drinks and margarine. LDL was 0.17 mmol/L higher than the oleic period. Two participants reported transient GI discomfort. Pressing method and resting tremor were not reported.

Poison-center reports include tremor and weakness after whole kernels. The same investigator observed no tremor in four experimentally exposed dogs. The overlapping series and trial are one lineage. Neither studied expressed oil, resting phenotype or Parkinson disease.

Thirteen Australian field cases described hindlimb weakness, recumbency and pain after reported raw or roasted kernels. The case series differs from the US poison-center lineage. It supplies no separate rest-tremor outcome.
Pure macadamia-oil application did not significantly change skin flare or erythema in the author abstract. The comparison involved skin application and no tremor assessment.
The published conservation consultation records traditional uses of the kernels for food and trade. No pressed oil preparation, symptom or comparative response is described.

The dissertation reports the registered oil-blend comparison. Eight people entered the macadamia arm and seven contributed interpretable hydrogen transit. The groups did not differ significantly in transit response. No movement outcome or pressing grade.

Seventeen participants per family-history group ate the same macadamia-oil meal. Postmeal metabolic responses did not significantly differ across groups. Pressing grade and tremor were unreported, and no oil-free comparator was included.

The distinct BRAVO comparison enrolled 125 and stopped early. It used macadamia-oil placebo against omega-3 and planned affect and cognitive assessments. The official registry has no posted results or Parkinson tremor outcome.

Protocol compares macadamia and coconut oils in a skin-absorption and metabolic context. Target enrollment was 16. Results and actual participant counts are absent from the official record. No food intake or tremor measure.

555 were randomized and 245 completed. Cognition, mood and resilience did not show clear group-by-time effects. The 2019 protocol, 2021 outcomes and later trainee analysis share a cohort. No untreated arm, pressing grade or rest observation is established.

One person reported less numbness and tingling after unrefined oil. A copied version and serving clarification duplicate the report. The record supplies no diagnosed Parkinson disease, movement endpoint or verified cold pressing.

The paper and reports describe two crossover samples of 16 and eight healthy students with separate figures. Acute alertness and fatigue contrasts do not estimate tremor. Outcome reports and the registry belong to the same family, and grade is unreported.

The abstract reports cerebellar staining and oxidative or inflammatory biomarker changes in a potassium-dichromate rat model. Full dosing, pressing grade and denominators remain unverified. The accessible text gives no interpretable motor or tremor result.

The Methods specify room-temperature hydraulic pressing. Comparative physicochemical and fatty-acid results establish process differences. The body and abstract attribute one percentage to different comparators. No participant or motor measure.

Eight of eleven historical Parkinsonian cases had tremor. Injected drug in oil and wax and oral belladonna lowered amplitude without materially changing incidence or rate. No oil-only exposure. The 1951 Ebin review is the same study family.

The 200-person clinical series covered several diagnoses. The author describes possible relief of painful rigidity with the injected drug and gives no individual tremor estimate or oil-only comparison.
Three of six animals received the drug dissolved in injected peanut oil. The reported effect is on levodopa-induced dyskinesia. Rest tremor appears in model description without an oil-only contrast.

Both diets contained peanut oil. The low rod yielded longer retention under the low-alpha-linolenic acid diet, the high rod and traction comparisons were inconclusive or unchanged, and some learning measures were weaker. No resting-tremor assessment.
The peanut-plus-rapeseed blend was the comparison for salmon-palm oil, with several dietary fatty acids changing. The fish-oil blend reduced general activity or changed habituation.

Six of sixty participants with peanut allergy reported reactions after crude oil, including two observable or measurable reactions. None reacted after the refined oil. Outcomes are acute allergy signs, with no identifiable rest-tremor response.

One trial assigned 129 healthy adults to eight weeks of peanut, olive, safflower oil or no study oil. The analyzed denominator for the activity result is unverified. Its companion paper reports no significant change in general activity, and neither report assessed tremor.
Measured fatty acids, tocopherols and phytosterols in specified cold-pressed oil. Availability of measured composition supplies no observed symptom contrast.
The table associates peanut-oil massage with infantile paralysis. This row identifies no direct witness, measured response or comparable oral route.
Table 2 records customary cooking and topical uses. Study citation counts measure use reports and cannot establish response or clinical effect.
The combined methanolic almond, peanut and watermelon seed extract favored less block catalepsy and greater activity. It did not test peanut oil, an isolated seed arm or a resting-tremor outcome.

The main report identifies oil-based control spread in healthy adults and tests cognition, stress and mood. Registration and later companion outcomes belong to the same intervention. No distinct oil-free comparator or tremor endpoint.

The ENHANce trial and nested TEMPUS-FUGIT use a peanut-oil omega-3 placebo in older adults with sarcopenia. The protocol and feasibility report address physical function, and the family has no separate Parkinson tremor result.
Metformin-treated outpatients consumed dietary oils including groundnut. The reported glucose and lipid outcomes do not record tremor or an acute hypoglycemic movement phenotype.
Shared diet in 16 patients includes cantaloupe. Supplement S2 and body Figure 4 score composite motor change. No fruit-level contrast, preparation or separate tremor estimate.
Same cohort as PMID23661325. Adjusted occurrence RR 1.00 (95% CI 0.72–1.38) combines four cucurbits. The indication is diagnosis occurrence and there is no separate raw-fruit comparison.
GliSODin favored memory in the restraint stress experiment. The supplemented mice were assessed for spatial learning and tissue endpoints.
A ripe pickling-melon versus muskmelon juice contrast concerns glycemia in people with diabetes. Neither a resting-tremor nor isolated raw flesh effect was reported.
Table 5 has a dose- and time-dependent pattern of rotarod means. Methods describe falls and the table gives time. Table 1 describes general behavior depression with no tremor item.
Table 3 gives shorter rotarod retention and Table 4 higher actophotometer activity. The abstract characterizes the rotarod as improved. The exposure is rind extract.
Crossover exposes volunteers to servings of separate unripe melon landraces or cucumber. Measured appetite and food reward without a tremor assessment.
The separate survey describes food experiences. Participant overlap with the crossover is unverified and its published outcomes do not inform rest tremor.

Mahlouji lists historical tremor and melon together only at the review level in separate tables. The Dadmehr textual analysis concerns a broader condition. Shared textual sources are plausible and no independent first-person response is established.
Rock melon is a named exposure in a registered crossover. Planned outcomes are glycemic index and load, and as of the review no results were available.
The capsule protocol lists frailty and quality-of-life outcomes. Registry results are absent and a named raw-fruit or resting-tremor comparison is not planned.
In mobility-limited older women, motor and fatigue differences are inconclusive. Capsules contain a Vauclusien melon extract and wheat gliadin.
Healthy men trained during a human supplement trial. The dried melon concentrate comparison did not give a clear between-group physical-fatigue difference or a separate tremor outcome.
A 61-participant healthy-adult comparison registered as NCT01767922 reports stress and fatigue. The proprietary freeze-dried concentrate and its endpoints cannot inform the frozen tremor outcome.

Regulatory review records tremor at the highest essential-oil toxicity exposure. The original case protocol and identity of the 2000 pamphlet animals remain open. Acute intoxication and toasted-fruit intake differ.
Oral methanolic fruit extract shortened experimenter-imposed bar posture. The assay did not score tremor.
Fresh leaf oil changed open-field and maze behavior in healthy mice. Separate five-animal limit screen disclosed no overt toxicity and gave no tremor count.

Oil group III shortened the bar posture relative to reserpine-only group II descriptively. Group IV was levodopa/carbidopa. Figures do not annotate the oil versus model comparison, and there was no item-level tremor.
Roasting changed the volatile profile, including lower fennel estragole. Full time, heat and sample-specific composition are open. No biological outcome was tested.
Cultivated and wild accessions differ greatly in starting volatiles, with a separate quantitative estragole estimate. The study has no roasting condition or symptom outcomes.
Whole crushed seed pellets lowered home-cage crossings and increased open-field center crossings. Toasting and resting tremor were outside the experiment.

The acute Table 1 records no convulsions or tremors in either fenchone or vehicle group. Methods and later table sample counts differ. The isolated compound comparison leaves the culinary Parkinson direction open.
A different methanolic extract had no reported deaths and no separately reported tremor outcome in the author abstract.
Boiled leaves and a separate claim about the fruit are documented under broad falij use. No firsthand fennel rest-tremor outcome or Parkinson diagnosis is identified.
Generalized seizure followed exposure to an unknown amount of fennel essential oil in cake in a person with epilepsy. No frozen outcome was recorded.
Repeated injections of leaf-and-stem juice were associated with convulsions. Route and dose units vary in the paper. No tremor outcome matches the claim.
Anethole given before rotenone improved rotarod and selected stride results. Resting tremor appears in the introduction as a disease feature.
Concentrated fruit extract reduced rotarod retention and grip in healthy mice. This does not identify a tremor phenotype.
Peri-lesion oral methanol extract favored coordination and grasp. Post-lesion-only comparisons were inconclusive. Neither was a tremor measurement.
Conference abstract gives rotarod, open-field and passive-avoidance results. Extract dosing and specific effect sizes remain open. The 2024 paper tests a separate in vivo challenge.
Oral fruit extract under LPS improved late coordination with no clear early result. No tremor assessment exists in the studied outcome set.
Tremors followed contaminated produce in cattle. Nitrate was measured in green and white plant waste and ruminal contents. No toasted seed or Parkinson exposure was isolated.
Fennel was held in a bundled seasoning oil during frying comparisons. The study measures aroma and composition without a separate fennel contrast.
The February conference abstract reports a concentration change in five people; the November Figure 4 lacks a plotted denominator. Treat the reports and Nomoto citation as one family for this review.
The clinical pilot assessed the separate rest item under cabergoline. No fruit was compared or measured.

Three people had lower UPDRS after antibiotic addition, with qualitative improvement in rest tremor or rigidity. Four were unchanged. The report gives no separated values for the item and the exposure is a different inhibitor.
The authors describe general motor improvements after itraconazole addition. One concentration and no separately reported resting-tremor change.
Whole fruit components and juice affected felodipine in a crossover. The food matrix effect cannot establish a comparable effect on cabergoline or symptoms.
Fresh white pulp changed measured exposure in healthy volunteers taking different calcium antagonists. No Parkinson drug or outcome was tested.
Grapefruit was listed in the mixed menu eaten by both Parkinson groups. No isolated ingredient or separate rest result.
The delay and severity description refer to an aggregate of induced signs. Timing of acute rat signs cannot specify resting-tremor severity.

Mean induced seizure tremor onset delayed in the drug-plus-juice arm versus drug plus water. The tested table comparator is the challenge-only arm. The stated denominator refers to the two beverage arms with nine rats each.
The registry concerns aroma and immediate brain signals or subjective responses. It gives no posted results.
The flavored drink observation does not describe a resting-tremor change. Regular grapefruit consumption, and added-sugar tremor, are different reports.
Injected isolated naringin and tissue degeneration in a rat model. No separate symptom sign.
The pretreatment and post-lesion comparisons separate tissue preservation from restoration in mice. No symptom measure.
Oral isolated limonin and general motor activity, with the exact task outcome requiring full methods.
The original isolated injection changed rod and pole behavior. Those tasks assess other motor functions, without a resting-tremor score.
The ground-soybean adjunct comparison gives longer ON and less dyskinesia. The abstract does not separate resting tremor or compare refined oil.
Spirography improved after both active octanol formulations. The pooled adverse-tremor and inconsistent six-hour results cannot isolate soybean oil.
Only the drug comparator varies against a shared oil vehicle. The prespecified essential postural tremor timepoint was inconclusive and later signals favor the drug.
Acoustic voice measures favored the active drug over the soybean-oil placebo. No oil-free placebo identifies a soybean oil effect and the refining grade is unspecified.

At day seven, 2.1 versus 4.7 (estimates read from Figure 4a) in highest oral whole-plant methanol-extract versus vehicle groups, eight mice per group. Fresh petioles carry identified extract compounds. Their effective dose and mediation in the mouse trial are unresolved.
The fresh petiole analysis found apigenin and luteolin also measured in the experimental extract. Chemistry supports an exposure link and supplies no independent symptom result.

Pharmaceutical butylphthalide compared off-medication tremor pooled across three types. The purported composite exceeds the stated maximum and nearly reproduces a quality-of-life row. The separate rest result cannot be interpreted.
One public contributor reported previous tremor, uncertain diagnosis and general benefit with seed extract, coffee and mannitol. No tremor change was attributed to a single exposure.

Two prints of one cohort's turkey frequency versus pooled self-reported tremor graphic. The tile is extremely close to zero on the positive side. Cooking, separate rest item, adjusted estimate, uncertainty and analyzed denominator are unverified.

Tremor returns in qualitative Figure 2 and 3 timelines after protein challenge in two participants. The third revised-load participant has no figure and the lower-load comparison has a different protocol. The authors give no specific rest score or baked exposure.

Five participants reported worsening general symptoms on an 80 g protein breakfast. Three also reported dyskinesia or restlessness with the high-carbohydrate meal. The balanced meal favored pegboard performance. No individual rest result or food ingredient is reported.

The author abstract separates a shorter response under the unusually high protein formula from inconclusive usual-allowance comparisons. There is no separate observed tremor subtype or comparable food preparation.

The Parkinson group showed supine hypotension and worsening of an aggregate motor score after a shared liquid meal. The twenty denominator refers to the Parkinson group rather than the sixteen controls.
Postprandial OFF time was shorter during the assigned low-protein product diet. The comparison supplies no separate rest measurement and cannot estimate an isolated baked-turkey effect.

An independently identifiable anecdote describes worse perceived medication effect during one holiday with repeated leftover turkey. Stronger attribution would require timing or food controls and a separately observed symptom. The quoted question counts as no additional observed event.

Six diet-alone participants and ten assigned the same fig-containing diet plus bowel cleansing. Preparation and individual consumption are missing. Motor totals, including Figure S2, do not provide a separate resting-tremor contrast.

A concentrated fruit extract reportedly favored general motor measures in haloperidol-treated rats. The available author abstract gives no item-level rest tremor estimate or active-exposure bridge to raw fruit. Keep full methods open.

Methods identify two bark formulations in 18 rats at assignment. Tables 11–13 are biochemical and have unclear analysis denominators. Discussion of a fruit-extract catalepsy result does not establish that arm in the experiment.
Groups of six per test received an aerial-part extract. Alertness and spontaneous activity fell, and rotarod time shortened. The assays lack a Parkinson or resting-tremor outcome.

A modern review lists Anjir and phenolic compounds as a potential Parkinson-related plant. Reference 20 leads toward fruit chemistry with bibliographic inconsistencies. No firsthand remedy or symptom outcome is available.

Three fresh fig cultivars had measured phenolics. The chemistry connects the traditional review's candidate reference to raw fruit, while there is no measured mediator match to the rat experiment or efficacy outcome.

Two copies of one graphic for the same cohort give a small inverse tile for unspecified olive oil and pooled self-reported tremor. There is no pairwise estimate, uncertainty, grade or separate rest item. The 2017 composite symptom analysis overlaps and has no separate tremor result.
Exact oil grade administered by injection improved rotarod and activity under toxin exposure. An acute tremor observation was outside the comparative endpoints.
The ketogenic recipes use extra-virgin olive oil. During the early phase, 12/24 versus 3/23 reported worsened tremor or rigidity. This is a bundled diet comparison with a combined adverse endpoint.
The oil association addresses Parkinson case status, with no within-disease separate tremor estimate or confirmed grade.

Table 2 shows one attenuation in ten tremor reports and prose mentions transient worsening without a count. The study selected volunteers; preliminary report overlap and separate rest outcomes remain open.
Named authors describe mustard among pungent dietary items and propose a general link to shaking. There is no firsthand treatment response.
Appendix A lists mustard within a menu. No ingredient comparison or separate rest result is reported.
Registered total scale and related white-seed enzyme formulation trail. Clinical use of the exact formulation and outcomes remain unverified.
An isolated compound with a registered total motor scale, unknown overall status and no posted results. There is no culinary-comparator premise.
Unheated brown powder added to cooked broccoli changes urinary metabolite recovery in healthy adults.
Measured raw and roasted black seed chemistry. Total glucosinolates fell. Preexisting isothiocyanate results were inconclusive.
Original bar, grip and coordination figures assess leaf extract. No rest-tremor rating or culinary seed comparison.
Relative glucosinolate signals declined after roasting. No measured Parkinson symptom or preparation-equivalent human dose.
The processed mustard adjunct raises measured urinary sulforaphane metabolite recovery. The study has no human Parkinson or rest-tremor outcome.

Sixty-one people randomized to isolated caffeine or placebo. UPDRS III rest tremor differed by -0.32 (95% CI -0.73 to 0.10) and -0.28 (-0.83 to 0.27) at weeks three and six. Both timepoints use the same trial. Tea chemistry confirms caffeine in the beverage with substantially smaller amounts per reported serving.

A caffeine dose escalation without an external comparator gives a within-group rest score reduction of 1.18 points at two weeks. Tremor worsening and physiological tremor occurred among discontinuation reasons. Twenty-five participants described, with substantial attrition.

Six percent of survey respondents with Parkinson perceived worse tremor with coffee. The same publication reports no clear increase after acute caffeine and does not give a separate compatible rest estimate. Group linkage and timing are unresolved, so no additional family count was assigned.

Brewed black tea averaged about 39 mg caffeine per 200 mL in cup-sized bags and 24 mg for loose leaf under those conditions, compared with 200 or 400 mg daily isolated caffeine in the clinical trial. Measured constituent bridge, with no symptom observations.
Some LRRK2 groups had favorable MDS-UPDRS II composite comparisons. The idiopathic comparison was inconclusive and a separate rest-tremor estimate was unavailable.
